profiles.meeting_scenario: A regional emergency management office is coordinating with a university research team to turn an emerging typology of multi-agency coordination into materials for an upcoming interagency workshop involving fire, police, public health, utilities, transport, and volunteer organizations. This check-in is a coordination meeting between the practice lead and the research program manager to align handoffs across workstreams: what artifact will go into next Wednesday's planning packet, what counts as the current workshop draft, who maintains the terminology support sheet, and how the shared repository will be used during final packaging. The agenda is to confirm Monday and Wednesday deliverables, make sure the workshop packet and research materials stay aligned, and avoid last-minute friction across the convening and research teams. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on who will provide which materials and when, while several second-order assumptions remain unspoken.

members.name: Dana Morales
members.expertise: Interagency planning, exercise design, emergency operations center coordination, stakeholder engagement
members.background: Dana has spent twelve years in county and regional emergency management, mostly translating doctrine into usable planning tools for mixed agency audiences and running coordination workshops after wildfire and flood seasons.
members.private_state: Dana wants a packet that agency representatives can use immediately without getting slowed down by research framing, and she is concerned that if the materials feel dense or provisional, some partner agencies will disengage before the pilot workshop.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot-ready' tool is something facilitators can put in front of agency participants next week with plain-language prompts and minimal explanation.
The 'workshop draft' means the streamlined practitioner-facing draft already previewed on the last steering call, which she assumes remains the operative version unless someone explicitly reopens it.
A 'glossary' is a short participant aid covering only terms likely to confuse agency attendees in the room.
If everything is kept in the shared folder, her office still assembles the participant-facing packet as the de facto final packaging authority because they are convening the event.

members.name: Dr. Liam Chen
members.expertise: Qualitative synthesis, framework development, evaluation design, knowledge translation for public-sector collaborations
members.background: Liam manages a multi-university project on interorganizational coordination and has been consolidating interview findings into a formal typology intended to become a diagnostic instrument with traceable dimensions and coding guidance.
members.private_state: Liam wants to preserve methodological integrity so the workshop yields interpretable feedback on the typology itself, and he worries that over-simplifying too early will make the outputs unusable for validation.
hidden_assumptions: A 'pilot-ready' tool is stable enough to function as a structured field test, with dimensions and wording fixed sufficiently to produce analyzable feedback.

The 'workshop draft' means the most recent master draft in the research repository, which he assumes automatically supersedes earlier preview materials even if everyone still uses the same shorthand label.
A 'glossary' should include the typology's full construct definitions and near-synonyms so facilitators and later coders interpret workshop language consistently.
If everything is kept in the shared folder, that folder acts as the single source of truth and edits should happen against master files rather than through downstream local packaging.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the typology materials should be 'pilot-ready' for next week's workshop.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes 'pilot-ready' means ready for live use by mixed agency participants: concise, easy to facilitate, and practical even if the underlying framework is still evolving.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes 'pilot-ready' means ready for a meaningful pilot of the instrument: dimensions, labels, and definitions stable enough that workshop feedback can be interpreted systematically.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely aiming at the same workshop and both naturally use 'pilot' language, so the phrase feels fully aligned; the divergence sits in the silent standard for readiness, not in any visible disagreement about the event.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to sending or packaging 'the workshop draft' or 'the latest draft.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the practitioner-oriented draft previewed during the steering call, which she treats as the workshop draft because that is the version stakeholders have already implicitly oriented around.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the updated master draft uploaded afterward in the research repository, which he also calls the workshop draft because it is the newest internally controlled version.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both artifacts are descendants of the same typology, both are plausibly 'latest' from each person's workflow, and both use the same colloquial label 'workshop draft,' so neither hears a version conflict when the phrase comes up.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to include a 'glossary' with the packet.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the glossary is a one-page participant support sheet limited to cross-agency terms that might stall discussion in the room.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the glossary includes the typology's conceptual vocabulary, definition notes, and nearby terms so workshop outputs can later be mapped back to the framework.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: A glossary sounds like a routine supporting artifact rather than a major planning decision, so both participants treat it as obvious and never surface the boundary question of who it is really for.

misalignment_points.topic: How the shared folder governs edits
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'keep everything in the shared folder' so everyone stays aligned.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the folder is a transparent handoff space where Liam deposits source materials and Dana's team pulls copies into its locally assembled planning packet.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the folder is the live document environment where the master files themselves are edited and preserved as the authoritative lineage for the workshop draft.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Shared folders are standard coordination infrastructure, so the statement sounds like simple good housekeeping; the hidden difference is about document lineage and edit authority, which neither person expects to need to spell out.

For me, pilot-ready means facilitators can use it next week with almost no setup: clear prompts, plain language, no research caveats getting in the way. If I can get clean materials by Monday, my team can package them with the agenda and keep partners engaged.

When I say the workshop draft, I mean the updated master version in the research repository, not the earlier preview.
